checks.title: Legacy authentication blocked
remediation: Check the sign-in logs for legacy protocol use (ID-016 lists the accounts) and move those accounts or devices to modern authentication.
Create an enabled policy for all users and all cloud apps with client app types Exchange ActiveSync clients and Other clients, grant control Block.
Exclude only the break-glass accounts.

userImpact.text: Old mail apps and devices using IMAP, POP or basic SMTP stop signing in; the sign-in log lists who uses them.

checks.narrative: Legacy protocols such as basic-auth IMAP, POP and SMTP cannot complete a multifactor prompt, so a password spray or a stolen password signs in without any second factor. Blocking them is the single control that removes most password-only sign-ins from the tenant. A policy in report-only mode or with a broad exclusion group leaves the door open for exactly the accounts an attacker will try.

checks.title: MFA required for all users
remediation: Create an enabled policy for all users and all cloud apps that requires multifactor authentication or an authentication strength.
Exclude only the break-glass accounts.
Move service accounts to workload identities or managed identities instead of excluding them.
Move any legacy exclusion group into a scoped policy with an end date.

userImpact.text: Every user answers MFA when they sign in, then not again on the same device for a while.

checks.narrative: A tenant-wide MFA policy is the baseline every other control assumes. Per-user MFA and security defaults cover fewer scenarios and cannot be scoped or reported on. Every account excluded from the policy is an account that signs in with a password alone, which is why the check counts a policy as passing only when its exclusions are limited to the break-glass accounts.

checks.title: Phishing-resistant authentication for administrator roles
remediation: Issue passkeys or FIDO2 keys to every administrator and have them register (AU-008).
Create an enabled policy that targets the privileged directory roles for all cloud apps and grants access only with the built-in Phishing-resistant MFA authentication strength.
Keep the break-glass accounts on a separate policy with the same strength.

userImpact.text: Administrators sign in with a passkey or security key; push and code approvals stop working for admin roles.

checks.narrative: Push notifications and one-time codes can be relayed by an adversary-in-the-middle kit, which captures the session as soon as the administrator approves. Phishing-resistant methods bind the credential to the site, so the relayed prompt fails. Administrators are the accounts those kits are aimed at, and the roles listed here are the ones Microsoft recommends protecting first.

checks.title: Risk-based policies for sign-in risk and user risk
remediation: Create a policy for all users and all cloud apps that requires multifactor authentication for medium and high sign-in risk.
Create a second policy that requires multifactor authentication and a secure password change for high user risk.
Exclude the break-glass accounts from both.
Run both in report-only mode for a week, watch the Identity Protection reports, then enable them.

userImpact.text: A user whose sign-in looks risky gets an extra MFA prompt; one whose account looks compromised changes their password.

checks.narrative: Identity Protection scores sign-ins and users on leaked credentials, anonymous networks, impossible travel and attacker infrastructure. Without a policy that acts on the score, the detections are a report nobody reads until after the incident. Requiring MFA on risky sign-ins and a password change on risky users turns the detection into an automatic response.

checks.title: Compliant device required for Office 365 on Windows and macOS
remediation: Confirm the Intune compliance policies and the Entra device registration state for Windows and macOS.
Create a policy for a pilot group targeting Office 365 on the Windows and macOS platforms that grants access only from a compliant device.
Widen it to all users once the pilot holds.

userImpact.text: Windows and Mac users without a compliant, enrolled device lose access to Office 365 until the device is enrolled.

checks.narrative: A stolen password with a valid MFA approval still lands on whatever machine the attacker chooses. Requiring a compliant device ties access to a managed, patched, encrypted endpoint with endpoint protection reporting in, which is the control that keeps session theft and credential phishing from turning into data access.

checks.title: No policy left in report-only mode
remediation: For each policy listed, review the report-only results in the sign-in logs and the Conditional Access insights workbook.
Enable the policy or delete it. A policy that cannot be enabled after a quarter is a design problem, not a monitoring one.

userImpact.text: What the report-only policy would have done starts happening; its report-only results show who.

checks.narrative: Report-only mode exists to measure impact before enforcing. A policy that stays in it for months protects nothing while looking like a control on the policy list. The pileup is a common finding in tenants where a rollout stalled, and it usually hides the policies that would matter most.

checks.title: Exclusion groups under the size threshold
remediation: For each group listed, review the membership and remove accounts that no longer need the exception.
Replace standing exclusions with a scoped policy that gives those accounts the right control instead of none.
Put an access review on the group.
Record any remaining exception with an owner and an expiry.

userImpact.text: Accounts removed from an exclusion group get the controls everyone else has, usually MFA.

checks.narrative: Every member of an exclusion group is outside the policy entirely. Groups created for a migration or a vendor tend to grow and never shrink, and an attacker who lands in one of those accounts faces no MFA at all. The size threshold is the point at which an exclusion stops being an exception and becomes a second, weaker policy.

checks.title: No MFA bypass for trusted locations
remediation: Remove the trusted-location exclusion from the MFA policies listed.
Where a specific system needs a location exclusion, scope it to that application and record the exception with an owner and an expiry.
Keep trusted locations for sign-in risk evaluation only.

userImpact.text: Users in the office answer MFA like everyone else, no more often than the sign-in frequency allows.

checks.narrative: Skipping MFA from the office network treats the network as the credential. Anyone on the wireless, a compromised device on the LAN, or a VPN session from a stolen laptop then signs in with a password alone. Zero trust guidance drops the location bypass because the perimeter is the easiest control to get behind.

checks.title: Sign-in frequency and non-persistent browser for administrators
checks.remediation: Create an enabled policy targeting the privileged directory roles for all cloud apps with the session controls sign-in frequency (for example 4 to 12 hours) and persistent browser session set to never persistent. Administrators then re-authenticate on a schedule and shared machines keep no admin session.

userImpact.text: Administrators sign in again every few hours, and browsers do not keep their admin session.

checks.narrative: An administrator session that persists for weeks is a token worth stealing. Limiting how long the session lives and preventing the browser from keeping it caps what a stolen cookie is worth, and it is the control that makes a token replay noticeable rather than silent.

checks.title: Token protection in use
remediation: Create a policy for all users targeting Exchange Online and SharePoint Online on the Windows platform with the session control Require token protection for sign-in sessions, in report-only mode.
Review the sign-in log for unsupported clients.
Enable the policy, recording a target date as an exception until then.

userImpact.text: Most Windows users notice nothing; unsupported apps fail to sign in until updated.

checks.narrative: Token protection binds the sign-in token to the device it was issued to, so a session cookie copied from a phished or malware-infected machine stops working elsewhere. It closes the gap that MFA leaves open once the user has already signed in. Client support is still growing, which is why report-only with a date counts here.

checks.title: Microsoft-managed policies not silently disabled
checks.remediation: For each Microsoft-managed policy listed as disabled, either enable it or confirm that an equivalent customer policy covers the same scenario and record that decision as an exception with an owner. Microsoft-managed policies cannot be deleted, so a disabled one is a standing decision that should be written down.

userImpact.text: Depends on the policy: most Microsoft-managed policies add an MFA prompt for a small group.

checks.narrative: Microsoft creates managed policies in tenants for the controls it considers baseline, such as MFA for administrators and for risky sign-ins, and enables them after a notice period. Disabling one without an equivalent policy removes a control the tenant was about to gain, and the state is easy to miss because the policy stays on the list.

checks.title: Break-glass accounts excluded from every blocking policy
remediation: Name the break-glass accounts in the profile and keep them in a dedicated group.
Exclude that group from every policy with a Block control.
Protect the accounts with a separate phishing-resistant policy and alert on their sign-ins.
Test one of them every quarter.

userImpact.text: Only the emergency accounts are affected; users see nothing.

checks.narrative: A blocking policy that applies to the break-glass accounts can lock every administrator out of the tenant at once, typically during the incident the policy was written for. A policy misfire, an MFA outage or a mistaken location change then has no way back in. Excluding the emergency accounts from every Block is what keeps Conditional Access recoverable.

checks.title: No policy references a deleted object
remediation: Open each policy listed and find the assignment, location or strength that no longer resolves.
Replace or remove it.
If the deleted object was an exclusion group, check who was in it, because those accounts are now inside the policy (or outside it, if it was an include).

userImpact.text: Users who fell inside or outside a policy because of the deleted object go back to the intended controls.

checks.narrative: When a group, user or named location a policy references is deleted, the policy keeps the orphaned id and silently stops covering or excluding whoever it pointed at. The portal shows nothing wrong. The result is a policy that reads correctly and does something different, which is the worst kind of drift.

checks.title: No policy left disabled past the threshold
remediation: Delete each policy listed, or document why it is kept disabled as an exception with an owner and an expiry.
Keep a copy of the policy JSON in the change record if the design might be needed again.

userImpact.text: Deleting a disabled policy changes nothing users see.

checks.narrative: Disabled policies accumulate from pilots and emergencies and make the policy list hard to read, which is how a reviewer misses the one that matters. A disabled policy can also be re-enabled by mistake with stale assignments. Either it is needed, and should be enabled, or it is not, and should go.

checks.title: Policy names follow the naming convention
remediation: Adopt a convention such as CA-<number>-<persona>-<control>; the Conditional Access document's naming report proposes a name for each policy.
Rename the policies listed.
Record the pattern in the profile (thresholds.namePattern) so the check enforces that exact pattern from then on.

userImpact.text: Renaming policies changes nothing users see.

checks.narrative: A naming convention is what lets a reviewer read a policy list and know what each policy is for without opening it. Tenants whose policies are named by whoever created them tend to have duplicates and gaps nobody noticed. With a pattern in the profile the check enforces it; without one it looks for a prefix-and-number structure across the names, and free-text names are the finding.

checks.title: Device code sign-in blocked
remediation: Create a Conditional Access policy for all users and all resources with the condition Authentication flows, Device code flow (and Authentication transfer), and the grant Block access.
Exclude only the break-glass accounts and a group for devices that really need device code sign-in (meeting room displays, some command-line work), and keep that group small.
Start in report-only mode for a week and check the sign-in log for device code sign-ins you did not expect.

userImpact.text: Almost no one notices. People who type a code at microsoft.com/devicelogin to sign in a TV, a shared display or a command-line tool are refused unless they are in the exception group.

checks.narrative: Device code phishing is a sign-in on the attacker's behalf: the attacker starts a device code sign-in with a trusted app, sends the code to a user as an urgent request, and the user signs in with MFA on the real Microsoft page, handing the attacker a token. MFA does not stop it because the user completes MFA. Few organisations need device code sign-in at all, so blocking it closes the attack for almost no cost.

checks.title: Registering a sign-in method is protected by Conditional Access
remediation: Create a Conditional Access policy for all users with the target User actions, Register security information.
Grant access only from a compliant or hybrid joined device, or require multifactor authentication and give newcomers a Temporary Access Pass for their first registration.
Exclude the break-glass accounts, start in report-only mode, and read the sign-in log for registrations the policy would have stopped.

userImpact.text: People add or change a sign-in method from a work device, or after proving who they are. A newcomer uses the Temporary Access Pass they are given.

checks.narrative: The page where a person adds an authenticator is the page an attacker wants most. With a stolen password and no rule on registration, the attacker registers their own phone on an account that has not set up MFA yet, and from then on passes every MFA prompt. A policy on that one action closes it.
